Thank you for this — the idea was right, and it's shipped in 0.16.0.

I changed the mechanism, and I want to be straight about why. Your version sent the state and questions to `/chat/completions` and asked a chat model to return JSON. That works, but what comes back is a language model's guess wearing a `confidence` number it made up. Everything in this repo reads that number as a calibrated probability — the 0.65 floor on a GUI action, the 0.7 floor before a transcript turn is dropped, "unsure is not hard" in the router — so an imitation would have quietly changed every one of those thresholds without failing anywhere visible.

It turns out OpenRouter serves the real Jev, through their Decisions API: `POST /api/alpha/decisions` with model `~typesafe/jev-latest`, and the body is `{model, state, questions}` — byte for byte the request TypeSafe takes. So your feature works exactly as you asked for it, one key instead of two, with no trade at all. Measured side by side on one decision: 433 ms through OpenRouter, 569 ms direct, same answer.

What landed, from your PR:

- `jev setup-key --provider openrouter`, storing under its own keychain service
- provider-aware `keystore`, with TypeSafe preferred when both keys exist (most machines here already have `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` set for a text model, and finding one shouldn't silently reroute decisions)
- `jev doctor` reporting `key.provider`

You're credited as co-author on the commit, and named in [CHANGELOG.md](https://github.com/kerpopule/hermes-jev-skills/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md) under 0.16.0.

One apology: `main` had its history rewritten a few hours ago, to remove a customer's name that had been committed by mistake. Every SHA changed, so this PR can no longer be merged as-is — that's my doing, not yours. Since the feature is in, I'll close this, but please do open another; the next one won't land on shifting ground.
Closing because the feature is in main as of 0.16.0 — see the note above. Thank you again, and please send another.

You are right, and thank you for the diagnosis — you found the exact line.

This was fixed in 0.16.0, which went out a few hours before you filed this, so you caught the repo mid-stride rather than got ignored. Your repro now returns the same `noul: 0.22` you got from the mapping form:

```console
$ echo '{"state":"The diff adds a null check and one unit test. No integration tests were run.","questions":[{"id":"merge","kind":"noul","text":"Is the evidence sufficient to merge this change?"}]}' | jev ask
{"answers": {"merge": {"type": "noul", "noul": 0.22}}, "usage": {"input_tokens": 292, "output_tokens": 20}, "latency_ms": 558}
```

`cmd_ask` now translates the vocabulary — `kind` → `type`, `text` → `instructions` — passes `criteria` through, and refuses a `choice` or `score` that arrives without criteria rather than letting the server reject it. Every other malformed input returns `{"error": "invalid_request", "detail": ...}` and exit 2 instead of a traceback.

Your point about the test suite was the more valuable half, and it was right: `AskQuestionShapeTests` mocked `client.ask`, so nothing checked what left the process, and one assertion pinned the spelling the API rejects. Those tests now run through `client.ask` with a fake transport and assert what goes on the wire.

You are named in the CHANGELOG under 0.17.0. If you hit anything else, please do file it — this one was exactly the right shape of report.

This is the most useful thing that has happened to this repo. Every one of these reproduced, and all of them are fixed in **0.17.0** — you are named in the CHANGELOG.

**The routing cache key.** Confirmed exactly as you describe, including that the guard on README line 102 holds only on a miss:

```
  1,000 tokens   -> cheap/tiny-v1    cached None
300,000 tokens   -> cheap/tiny-v1    cached True        <- a 32k window
300,000, cache off -> mid/general-v2  "no simple model fits this turn"
```

The key now carries a coarse context bucket — `(4k, 16k, 32k, 64k, 128k, 200k, 400k, 1M)`, and anything larger is its own class — so a repeat inside the same bucket still costs one Jev call while a grown session misses. You were also right that the key omitted the config: it now includes a fingerprint of `tiers`, `exclude`, `escalate` and `sticky_context_tokens`, so editing `routing.json` takes effect without a restart.

**Compaction batching.** Also confirmed. On a mixed transcript one 40-turn batch encoded to 120,601 characters against the 60,000 limit. `_pack` now packs by encoded size, reusing the rule `rerank.py` already had, and — the half that made it dangerous — a run where some batches failed reports **`partial`** with the ids left `unjudged`, instead of `ok`. `jev-compaction/SKILL.md` now tells an agent to treat `partial` like `fail_open`.

**The clipped `ask`.** You were right, and it was worse than the risk floor alone: `privacy.is_sensitive` ran on the same clipped copy, so a secret in the middle of a long paste also decided whether the turn's text was sent at all. Both now read the whole turn. Clipping is for what Jev reads, never for what we check.

**The smaller ones, all corrected.** `ceil(N/120) + 1` requests, not "two" — and your distinction between round trips and billed requests is now in the skill text, because it is the number people pay for. README says 2,500 characters. And the point about `redacted-text` mode versus the instruction the plugin injects is fair and was the hardest to argue with: the README now says plainly that on an automatically routed turn the agent has no say, and `private_profiles` is the actual control.

**CI.** Found independently the same day and fixed a few hours before your report — `opener=subprocess.run` as a default argument, exactly as you diagnosed. Your guess about macOS was right: those tests were "passing" by opening System Settings on the author's machine. It is green now, on Ubuntu and macOS, 3.9 and 3.13.

**On the redactor:** agreed, and I would rather state the scope than widen the regexes indefinitely. A card number, an international phone number and an unlabelled credential are caught now; a CRM id and an internal IP are not, and that is the honest boundary of a pattern-matcher.

> Happy to send a PR for any of these.

Please do — and for what it is worth, a PR from you would be read carefully. `CONTRIBUTING.md` now opens with the two traps that have caught everyone here, including the default-argument one you found. If you are writing that piece, the numbers above are all reproducible from the tests in `tests/test_reported_bugs.py`, which exist because of this issue.

Checked all of it against HEAD rather than from the issue being closed. It holds, and two of the fixes are better than what I asked for.

**The cache key.** `route.py:441`'s config fingerprint over `tiers`, `exclude`, `escalate` and `sticky_context_tokens` is something I hadn't thought to ask for — I only reported the missing context size. A routing config that takes effect without a restart is the more useful half of that change. The bucket ladder (4k…1M, larger as its own class) is the right granularity: coarse enough that a repeat inside a bucket still costs one call, fine enough that a session growing past a model's window misses.

**Compaction.** `compact.py:107`'s three-way status with the `unjudged` list is exactly right, and having `jev-compaction/SKILL.md` tell the agent to treat `partial` like `fail_open` closes the loop I was actually worried about — the packer alone would have left a smaller version of the same problem.

**The clipped `ask`.** You found something worse than I reported and said so plainly. `privacy.is_sensitive` reading the clipped copy meant a secret past the cut decided whether the turn was sent *at all* — that's a failure in the direction that matters, and I missed it. The comment at `route.py:522` ("What is clipped is what Jev reads, never what we check") is the invariant stated properly.

**CI.** Green on Ubuntu and macOS, 3.9 and 3.13, and `tests/test_reported_bugs.py` exists. Worth noting for anyone reading later: you found the `subprocess.run` default-argument bug independently, a few hours before my report landed — including that those tests had been "passing" by opening System Settings on your machine. I'm crediting it that way in the write-up rather than as something the report caused.

**On the redactor.** I think stating the scope beats widening the regexes, and I'd rather a pattern-matcher with an honest boundary than one that implies completeness. A CRM id and an internal IP genuinely aren't catchable this way.

The review on mrjev.com now carries all of this as an update section. I've kept the original findings above it rather than rewriting them away, so the sequence stays readable.

> a PR from you would be read carefully

I read `CONTRIBUTING.md`; leading with the two traps that have caught everyone, including the default-argument one, is a good use of that file.

Checked this against Hermes' own plugin loader, because I hit the same symptom (installed and
enabled, nothing routing) and wanted to know whether the registration was the cause.

The middleware name is **valid**, so this specific cause does not hold:

- `ctx.register_middleware("llm_request", ...)` is validated against `VALID_MIDDLEWARE`
  (`hermes_cli/middleware.py`), which is `{tool_request, tool_execution, llm_request, llm_execution}` —
  `LLM_REQUEST_MIDDLEWARE = "llm_request"`. `pre_llm_call` and `transform_llm_output` are both members of
  `VALID_HOOKS` in `hermes_cli/plugins.py`.
- Registration of an *unknown* key is not silent: `_track_callback` logs
  `Plugin '<name>' registered unknown <kind> '<key>' (valid: ...)` and then stores it anyway. So a bad
  name would leave a warning, not a quiet no-op.
- On my install no such warning appears in the logs.

So the routing is not dead *by this mechanism*. In my case the actual cause was simpler: the gateway
process had not been restarted since installing, so the plugin was never loaded, and routing is
shadow/off by default anyway. Worth confirming which of those it is here before changing the hook name —
happy to share the exact commands if useful.

Noticed #5 while writing this up — same bug, same fix, closed by its own author the same
day it was opened. Two things I checked before assuming it was a rejection, in case they
are useful here:

- **Upstream `main` still has the bug.** `git show origin/main:install.py` still has
  `block.insert(key + 1, f"  - {name}")` at line 216, so #5 was not closed because it
  landed some other way.
- **Its failure looks like `action_required`, not a real test failure.** Every external PR
  on this repo shows `action_required` (maintainer approval needed before CI runs), and #5
  is the only one that actually ran — because you authored it, so CI started automatically.
  I could not read its logs (`log not found`, expired), so I checked out its commit and ran
  all three CI commands on that code myself: `unittest discover -s tests` (770 OK),
  `unittest discover -s router-dashboard/tests` (70 OK) and `check_release.py` (clean), on
  both macOS 3.14 and 3.9.6. All pass, so nothing in its diff was actually broken. My guess
  is an older base plus `pyyaml` not being installed in the first job, but I cannot prove
  that from here — worth a look if you are diffing the two.

Difference between the two, for whatever it is worth: #5 resolves the indent with a regex
helper that also scans forward from the `enabled:` key; mine takes the indent of the first
item line in the block and falls back to two spaces. Behaviour is the same on every config
I tried (empty list, missing section, 2-space, 4-space, mixed) — happy to rebase onto
whatever shape you prefer, or drop this one if you would rather land the original.

Both new tests here assert on the parsed list rather than the text. The correct and the
broken output differ by two spaces of indentation, so a text assertion passes either way —
that is how this got in.

## Closing — author is correct

Thank you for the correction, you're right on both counts and I was wrong.

I re-read the plugin source and you're correct: line 360 of `plugins/hermes-jev/__init__.py` calls

```python
ctx.register_middleware("llm_request", _on_llm_request)
```

not `register_hook`. And `llm_request` IS in `VALID_MIDDLEWARE` at `hermes_cli/middleware.py:21,25` (alongside `tool_request`, `tool_execution`, `llm_execution`). The plugin source and `plugin.yaml` are correct.

On the "silent failure" claim — I was partly right and partly wrong. The "unknown key" warning in `_track_callback` does fire, but only when the name is not in the valid set, which is not the case here. So registration of `llm_request` as middleware does not warn and does proceed.

### What was actually wrong on my end

The real root cause turned out to be a local config bug in `~/.hermes/config.yaml`. The relevant block looked like this:

```yaml
plugins:
  enabled:
  - hermes-handoff
  - hermes-jev
    - <other plugins indented under hermes-jev>
```

PyYAML parses that as `[hermes-handoff, {hermes-jev: [<other plugins>]}]` — `hermes-jev` was orphaned as a parent of a nested list rather than a peer of `hermes-handoff`. The plugin manager's gate (`gate_manifest`, line ~218 of `plugins_discovery.py`) does `names & enabled` as a set intersection, and since `hermes-jev` was not a clean element of `plugins.enabled`, the gate returned `Skipping 'hermes-jev' (not in plugins.enabled)` and `register(ctx)` was never called. No hooks, no middleware, no routing — exactly the symptom we both observed.

After dedenting so `hermes-jev` is a peer of `hermes-handoff`:

```yaml
  enabled:
    - hermes-handoff
    - hermes-jev
    - <other plugins at same indent>
```

`discover_plugins()` now reports `hermes-jev enabled=True error=None`, `mgr._middleware["llm_request"] -> 1 callback`, plus the expected hook registrations. The plugin's source and your registration pattern are correct; the bug was entirely on my side.

### What your comment correctly diagnosed

> "In my case the actual cause was simpler: the gateway process had not been restarted since installing, so the plugin was never loaded, and routing is shadow/off by default anyway."

In your case "the plugin was never loaded" was the right explanation because something in your install process meant the gate rejected it. In my case it was a config YAML indentation issue — same gate, same symptom, different upstream cause. The plugin code, your hook/middleware surface design, and your registration pattern are all fine.

### Closing this issue

The plugin is not broken; the original report was a misdiagnosis on my part. Closing as `not a bug` / user error. Sorry for the noise.

One more data point for why this matters: TypeSafe's own official agent skill — [`typesafe-ai/skills` → `skills/typesafe-ai/SKILL.md`](https://github.com/typesafe-ai/skills/blob/main/skills/typesafe-ai/SKILL.md), the one their docs tell Claude Code and Codex users to install — writes its description as a block scalar:

```yaml
name: typesafe-ai
license: MIT
description: >
  Build AI-powered software with TypeSafe: small units of AI intelligence you
  can use like programming primitives. ...
```

On `main`, `_front_matter` reads that as `description: ">"`, so the picker ranks TypeSafe's reference skill on the string `typesafe-ai: >` and nothing else. With this PR it gets the 500-character description its authors wrote.

Follow-up commit pushed — the first pass was incomplete.

`_BLOCK_SCALARS` was a fixed set of eight strings. YAML lets the indentation and chomping indicators appear in either order, so `>2-`, `|+2`, `>-2` and `|2+` are all valid headers the set misses, and the comparison was against the whole remainder of the line, so `description: > # folded` missed too. An unrecognised header falls through to the plain `key: value` branch — which is the exact bug this PR is about: the description becomes the marker and the skill reaches Jev with nothing to be ranked on.

Now it matches the shape (`^[>|][0-9+-]*\s*(?:#.*)?$`), and a block ends on the first non-blank line less indented than the block's own first line rather than on the next line containing a colon.

One deliberate choice worth flagging: `|` is normalised to a single line like `>`, not kept with its breaks. Strict YAML would keep them, but both go to the same consumer, which truncates the description to a few hundred characters and lists it for a decision model — the author's line breaks carry nothing the reader can use, and `>` already folds blank lines away in this implementation. A test pins that so it is a decision rather than an accident; happy to switch it if you would rather be YAML-exact.

4 new tests, all red against the previous commit (7 subtest failures). Full suite: 803 passed, 1 skipped. `scripts/check_release.py` clean.

Confirmed from the field — same root cause, worse variant. An install here fused **11** plugins into one string instead of dropping one.

Before (2-space indent from a previous manual edit):
```yaml
plugins:
  enabled:
  - hermes-handoff
  - hermes-jev
```

After install.py:
```yaml
plugins:
  enabled:
  - hermes-handoff
  - hermes-jev
    - argos-status
    - browser-browser-use
    ... (11 more)
```

Valid YAML, parses fine, `hermes config get plugins.enabled` returned `['hermes-handoff', 'hermes-jev - argos-status - browser-browser-use - ...']` — one folded string. argos-status, chrome-profiles, tool-compactor, web-defuddle, web/ddgs, web/searxng and the rest all showed "not enabled" in `hermes plugins list` while everything looked installed.

Repaired with `hermes config set plugins.enabled '[...13 names...]'` and verified as a real list. Adding to the fix rationale: the 2-space style (dash at the same indent as the `enabled` key) is also valid YAML that Hermes itself writes, so the installer must detect the existing style, not assume 4-space.

Independent confirmation from a real install, plus one downstream symptom worth recording.

**What `plugins.enabled` looked like in a pre-repair backup:** a 10-item list in which **one item is a single string holding nine names joined by `" - "`**:

```
[3] hermes-jev - browser-obscura - hermes-telemetry - obsidian-memory - platforms/buzz - ponytail - token-optimizer - tool-slimmer - web-search-plus
```

Notes on that artefact, offered as data rather than a diagnosis:
- it includes `ponytail`, which matches no installed plugin on this box (a phantom name inside the folded string);
- the same names also appear as individual list items in the same list, so the corruption produced a *junk entry alongside* valid ones, at least at the moment this backup was taken;
- two backups were written seconds apart (`...104107`, `...104120`), so this one may already sit mid-repair — treat the ordering accordingly.

**The symptom it produced, and why it was hard to trace:** the plugin that stopped loading was this one (`hermes-jev`), and its own `plugins.entries.hermes-jev` block was intact, so reading the config looked healthy. What actually surfaced was far away from the cause — the gateway rejected `/jev` as an unknown slash command and none of the plugin's tools (`jev_supervise`, `jev_choose_action`, `jev_compact_select`, ...) appeared in the live tool catalog.

**Operational note that cost the most time:** repairing `plugins.enabled` does nothing for an already-running gateway. The process had loaded plugins at startup, so it kept the old set; comparing gateway uptime against the timestamp of the config repair is the first thing to check. After a restart, `/jev` worked on the first try.

Also: `hermes plugins enable <name>` can add entries but the CLI has no command to remove a junk one, so the folded string can only be cleared with a surgical line edit — and never through a YAML round-trip, which destroys every comment in `config.yaml`.

One edge in the landed code, found while comparing and not exercised by either branch — flagging it, not proposing work: `enable_plugins` now accepts an `enabled:` key at any depth inside the block, so a nested one with no value or an empty inline list is treated as `plugins.enabled`:

```yaml
plugins:
  entries:
    enabled: []
```

comes out as

```yaml
plugins:
  entries:
    enabled:
    - hermes-handoff
    - hermes-jev
```

so the names go to `plugins.entries.enabled` and no `plugins.enabled` is created; with the previous two-space-only match, a new `plugins.enabled` was written instead (checked against `e797a04`). Whether that shape occurs in practice is your call — mentioned because "unfamiliar YAML stays untouched" is the stated intent, and this one is edited rather than refused.

Thank you, Timo. This was a real gap, and the reproduction made it easy to confirm. The fix is on main as b3f7418, with a follow-up test fix in 7e7278c. CI passed on all 4 jobs (Ubuntu and macOS, Python 3.9 and 3.13): run 36223107355. You are credited with a `Co-Authored-By` trailer and in the CHANGELOG.

**What landed from your change:**

- `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` can now carry a path prefix, so `https://gw.example/jev` becomes `https://gw.example/jev/v1/systemone`. A prefix must be plain path segments: no `..`, `%`, spaces or empty segments. That keeps the URL we check identical to the URL we request.
- A gateway that requires a bearer now has a supported configuration.

**The one thing I changed, and why:** you asked the open question directly, so here is a direct answer. The bearer comes from a new, dedicated variable, `JEV_PROXY_API_KEY`, not from `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`.

For most installs, `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` in the environment *is* their real TypeSafe key, because it is the first place `keystore.resolve` looks. Forwarding it would have started sending a provider key to whatever host `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL` names. That would happen on every existing install that has both variables set, with nobody opting in. It would also silently narrow the #15 guarantee, which is still "no provider key ever reaches an override".

A dedicated variable costs a LiteLLM setup one extra line. It also means that key can only reach the gateway it was set for.

Details:

- It is read from the environment only (never the keychain or the credentials file) and sent only to the override.
- Your test cases survive with one inversion: an https override with only `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` set now asserts that *no* `Authorization` header is sent.
- I also allowed the prefix and the bearer on numeric-loopback `http`, for a local gateway such as LiteLLM on 127.0.0.1. Plaintext to anything else is still refused.

**The "fails silently" half:**

- `jev doctor` now names the override and says whether a bearer goes with it.
- It asks the override even when no key is stored.
- It exits non-zero when the override is invalid or refuses the call.

So your 401 now shows up as `"jev": {"reachable": false, "error": "auth_failed"}`.

**The four local failures you flagged were real, and they were ours:**

- `SkillHookRootTests` ×3 fail wherever Hermes is importable. The plugin asks Hermes for its skill roots, and the test did not stop it. We saw the same three failures under our own Hermes venv.
- The GUI credential-isolation test's "no key" case fails when an OpenCode Zen key or `JEV_PROVIDER` is in the environment. I reproduced it with a synthetic Zen key.

Both are isolated in 7e7278c. The suite now passes under both conditions.

Closing this as integrated, and #23 with it. If `JEV_PROXY_API_KEY` does not fit your gateway, please reopen or file a new issue and we will look again.

Thanks — that is a real counting error on my side, in two places, and one of them changes the numbers. No extra samples: all three runs scored the same 20 turn IDs (the same 12 `needs a skill` turns and 8 `needs none`). I recomputed everything below from the saved per-turn records.

**Why the cells sum to 21/22 instead of 20.** I scored this as a binary decision — a skill is suggested or it is not. 20 turns = 12 positives + 8 negatives. A positive turn that receives the *wrong* skill is simultaneously a false negative (the right skill was missed) and a false positive (a wrong one was offered), so it increments two cells. That happens on 2 turns in the 951-catalog run (hence 22) and on 1 turn in the pruned run (hence 21). Precision and recall are computed from the cells, not from their sum, so the convention does not inflate either metric — but the row should have said so, and I will report the 20-turn decomposition alongside the cells from now on.

**The pruned row was also wrong in a way that matters.** For that row I took TP from the ungated `label == top1` matches — 7 of them — instead of applying the two gates. One of those turns (`online-grocery-shopping`, `needs_skill` 0.09, `match` 0.15) is rejected by both thresholds, so it is a false negative, not a hit. Recomputed from the same records, same 20 turns, same labels:

| need / match | TP | FP | FN | TN | precision | recall |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.50 / 0.50 (current default) | 6 | 5 | 6 | 4 | 0.55 | 0.50 |
| 0.60 / 0.60 | 6 | 3 | 6 | 6 | **0.67** | 0.50 |

So the corrected reading is: pruning at the shipped 0.50/0.50 takes precision 0.45 -> 0.55 (+0.10, not +0.19) with recall 0.42 -> 0.50, and raising both gates to 0.60 on the pruned catalog takes 0.55 -> 0.67 (+0.12, not +0.14) with recall flat. Both effects hold in direction; I overstated the magnitudes, and the 0.78 figure should be read as 0.67.

The 951-catalog row reproduces exactly as posted (5 / 6 / 7 / 4, 0.45 / 0.42) and is unaffected — that row did apply the gates to TP.

**Your failure-mode question, measured.** At 0.60/0.60, zero of the 12 skill-needed turns had the correct skill as top-1 with `match` >= 0.60 while `needs_skill` fell below 0.60 — so in this sample no correct proposal was suppressed by the raised need gate. All six false negatives are turns the model itself scored below the gate:

- `needs_skill` 0.09, 0.24, 0.38, 0.41, 0.45 — silence, with the right skill not retrieved at all in four of the five;

The precision gain from 0.50 -> 0.60 comes from dropping two unnecessary suggestions on no-skill turns (`needs_skill` 0.51 and 0.58), not from blocking correct ones.
